His deeply sunburned face was largely concealed by whiskers and mustache. He carried an enormous oak cudgel, but seemed otherwise without weapons. With a clumsy bow he wished us “good evening” in French; his accent, though touched with Neufchatel, clearly suggested that he came originally from Paris.

“Take a seat, my friend,” said Dupin. “I imagine you have come concerning the Ourang-Outang. Upon my honour, I almost envy your ownership of him. He is a splendid creature and doubtless worth a great deal. What age would you judge him to be?”

The sailor breathed deeply, like a man freed from an unbearable weight, and answered with renewed confidence:

“I can't say for certain, but he mustn't be above four or five years old. Is he here?”

“Oh, no; we had nowhere suitable to keep him. He is at a livery stable close by in the Rue Dubourg. You may collect him to-morrow morning. Naturally, you can establish that he belongs to you?”

“Certainly I can, sir.”

“I shall regret giving him up,” Dupin remarked.

“I wouldn't have you go to all this trouble without payment, sir,” said the fellow. “Couldn't expect that. I'm quite willing to give a reward for finding the animal—anything reasonable, I mean.”

“Well,” my friend answered, “that is perfectly fair. Let me consider what I should ask. Ah! I have it. This shall be my reward: you will tell me everything you know about the murders in the Rue Morgue.”

Dupin uttered these last words quietly, in a very low voice. With equal composure he went to the door, locked it, and slipped the key into his pocket. Then he took a pistol from his breast and, without the slightest agitation, laid it upon the table.

The sailor's face reddened as though he were choking. He sprang up, clutching his cudgel; but almost at once he sank back into the chair, shaking violently, with a face like death. Not a word escaped him. I pitied him with all my heart.

“My friend,” Dupin said gently, “you are frightening yourself without cause; indeed you are. We mean you absolutely no harm. On my honour as a gentleman and a Frenchman, I promise that we intend no injury to you. I know perfectly well that you are innocent of the horrors committed in the Rue Morgue. Still, you cannot reasonably deny that you are connected with them to some extent.

“Goodbye, Uncle George. If I stay any longer, I'll be late for lunch. Thank you for the information. I always want to know everything about my new friends and nothing about my old ones.”

“Where are you having lunch, Harry?”

“At Aunt Agatha's. I've invited myself and Mr. Gray. He's her latest protégé.”

“Humph! Tell your Aunt Agatha to stop troubling me with her charitable appeals. I'm sick of them. The woman seems to think I have nothing to do except write checks for her foolish enthusiasms.”

“All right, Uncle George. I'll tell her, but it won't make any difference. Philanthropists lose all sense of humanity. It's their defining trait.”

The old gentleman grunted his approval and rang for his servant. Lord Henry walked through the low arcade into Burlington Street and headed towards Berkeley Square.

So that was the story of Dorian Gray's parents. Crude as the telling had been, its suggestion of a strange, almost modern romance had moved him. A beautiful woman risking everything for a reckless passion. A few wild weeks of happiness ended by a vile, treacherous crime. Months of silent anguish, followed by a child born in pain. The mother taken by death, the boy left alone under the tyranny of a loveless old man. Yes, an interesting background. It set the young man in relief, made him more perfect, in a way. Something tragic lay behind everything exquisite. Worlds had to suffer labor pains for even the humblest flower to bloom.... And how charming he had been at dinner the previous evening, sitting opposite him at the club, eyes startled and lips parted in frightened delight, while the red candle shades deepened the rose of dawning wonder in his face. Talking to him was like playing a superb violin. He responded to every touch and vibration of the bow.... There was something dangerously fascinating in exercising influence. Nothing else resembled it. To project your soul into a graceful form and let it linger there; to hear your intellectual convictions returned with all the added music of youth and passion; to pour your temperament into another person like a subtle liquid or an unfamiliar perfume—there was real pleasure in that. Perhaps it was the most satisfying pleasure left in an age as narrow and vulgar as theirs, so crudely sensual in its enjoyments and so commonplace in its ambitions.... This young man, whom chance had so unexpectedly brought into his life at Basil's studio, was a remarkable specimen, too. Or at least he could be shaped into one.

Plenty of cold water remained with which to conclude their feast. After a while Becky proposed that they start moving again. Tom said nothing for a moment. Then he asked:

“Becky, could you stand hearing something I've got to tell you?”

Her face lost its colour, but she thought she could.

“Well, Becky, then we've got to remain here, where there's drinking water. That little stump is the last candle we have!”

Becky broke into sobs and cries. Tom tried his best to soothe her, with little success. Finally she said:

“Tom!”

“What, Becky?”

“They'll notice we're missing and come looking!”

“Yes, of course! They certainly will!”

“Perhaps they're looking already, Tom.”

“Why, maybe so. I hope they are.”

“When would they notice, Tom?”

“When they reach the boat, I suppose.”

“But it might be dark then. Would they see that we weren't there?”

“I can't tell. Anyhow, your mother would miss you the minute they got home.”

The fear that crossed Becky's face recalled Tom to himself, and he realized his mistake. Becky was not supposed to return home that night! Both children fell silent, thinking. Presently another outburst of grief showed him that she, too, had understood the thought troubling him: Sunday morning might be half over before Mrs. Thatcher learned that Becky was not at Mrs. Harper's.

They fixed their eyes upon the scrap of candle, watching it slowly, mercilessly melt. At last only half an inch of wick remained standing. They saw the weak flame rise and sink, creep up the slender thread of smoke, and hover briefly at its summit. Then the terror of complete darkness took possession of the place.

Neither could say how much time had passed before Becky gradually realized that she was weeping in Tom's arms. They knew only that, after an interval which seemed endless, they both emerged from a heavy stupor of sleep to face their misery anew. Tom said it could be Sunday now, or even Monday. He attempted to draw Becky into conversation, but sorrow overwhelmed her and she had lost every hope. Surely they had been missed long since, Tom said; people must be searching. He would call out, and perhaps somebody would hear. He tried, but the far-off echoes sounded so dreadful in the darkness that he did not repeat it.

Hour after hour slipped away, and hunger once more troubled the prisoners. Some of Tom's half of the cake was still left. They shared and ate it, yet seemed more hungry afterwards than before.
